nationality_or_literary_tradition: American-British; the modernist long poem, the verse drama and the criticism of tradition
literary_identity: Poet, dramatist and critic; the author of The Waste Land and Four Quartets, the most influential poet-critic of the century, and the Nobel laureate of 1948.
biography: Born Thomas Stearns Eliot in St Louis, Missouri, on 26 September 1888 into a Unitarian family of New England descent; he studied at Harvard, Paris and Oxford, settled in London in 1915, married Vivienne Haigh-Wood in 1915, worked in Lloyds Bank (1917–25) and edited The Criterion (1922–39). Prufrock and Other Observations appeared in 1917, The Waste Land in 1922, The Hollow Men in 1925; he became a British subject and an Anglo-Catholic in 1927, published Ash-Wednesday in 1930, Murder in the Cathedral in 1935, Four Quartets in 1943 and won the Nobel Prize in 1948. He died in London on 4 January 1965.
literary_profile: Eliot changed the language of English poetry. The Waste Land made the fragment, the quotation and the mythic parallel the instruments of modern verse; Four Quartets is the period's great religious poem; and his criticism — 'Tradition and the Individual Talent', 'The Metaphysical Poets', 'Ulysses, Order, and Myth' — invented the vocabulary in which modern literature has been discussed ever since. As editor of The Criterion and as a director of Faber and Faber he shaped what modernism published.
stylistic_characteristics: The abrupt juxtaposition of registers and quotations; the objective correlative and the avoidance of direct statement; free verse organised by the musical phrase; the dramatic monologue and the dramatic lyric; the allusion that carries the argument; the flat conversational tone broken by sudden lyric intensity.
intellectual_concerns: The waste land and the decline of the West; time, memory, and the moment of incarnation; doubt, faith, and the via negativa; the modern city and the crowd; sex without love and the failure of desire; tradition and the individual talent; the theatre and the ritual of the church.
historical_significance: Eliot is the central poet and critic of the period: The Waste Land is the defining poem of modernism, Four Quartets its great religious meditation, and his criticism set the canon and the vocabulary of the twentieth century. He is the only writer of the period who is equally decisive as poet, critic, editor and dramatist.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: American; imagism, the modernist epic and the translation as form
literary_identity: Poet, critic and translator; the founder of Imagism and Vorticism, the editor of The Waste Land, and the author of the Cantos — the most influential and most contested American poet of the century.
biography: Born Ezra Loomis Pound at Hailey, Idaho, on 30 October 1885; he studied at Hamilton College and the University of Pennsylvania, taught briefly, and left for Europe in 1908, settling in London (1908–20), Paris (1921–24) and Rapallo (1924–45). In London he founded Imagism (1912), edited Blast (1914), wrote Cathay (1915) and Hugh Selwyn Mauberley (1920), and cut The Waste Land down to its published form. He broadcast for Mussolini during the war, was indicted for treason, and was confined in St Elizabeths Hospital, Washington, from 1946 to 1958, where he completed Rock-Drill and Thrones. He died in Venice on 1 November 1972.
literary_profile: Pound is the single greatest force in the making of modern poetry in English. His manifesto of Imagism taught the century to write free verse; Cathay (1915) invented the modern translation-poem; Mauberley is the finest short sequence of the period; and the Cantos, begun in 1915 and left unfinished in 1972, are the period's attempt at the American epic. As editor, talent-spotter and controversialist he made the careers of Eliot, Joyce, Frost, H.D. and Hemingway possible.
stylistic_characteristics: The image as the unit of the poem; the line composed by the musical phrase; the ideogram and the juxtaposition without connectives; translation as a mode of original composition; the collage of document, quotation and satire in the long poem; the vorticist economy of language.
intellectual_concerns: The modern city and the usura of the money economy; the American past and the epic of the republic; Confucius and the order of the state; art, patronage and the artist's place; love, desire and the troubadour inheritance; the betrayal of the intellect by the market.
historical_significance: Pound is the central maker of modernism: he taught the age to write free verse, edited The Waste Land into its permanent form, discovered and published the writers who changed the century, and spent fifty years on the Cantos. His politics were catastrophic and his influence was decisive; both facts are part of the record.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: American; the imagist lyric, the long poem and the modernist woman's epic
literary_identity: Poet and novelist; the finest poet of Imagism and the author of Trilogy, one of the great long poems of the Second World War.
biography: Born Hilda Doolittle in Bethlehem, Pennsylvania, on 10 September 1886 into a Moravian family; she studied at Bryn Mawr, travelled to Europe in 1911, and was named 'H. D., Imagiste' by Pound in 1912. She married Richard Aldington in 1913, published Sea Garden (1916), had a daughter by Cecil Gray in 1919, and began a long relationship with the novelist Bryher; she lived in Switzerland and London, was analysed by Freud in 1933–34, and wrote Trilogy during the London Blitz (published 1944–46) and Helen in Egypt (1961). She died in Zurich on 27 September 1961.
literary_profile: H. D. is the purest poet of Imagism and one of the most important women writers of the period. Sea Garden gave the movement its permanent texts; her later long poems — Trilogy, Helen in Egypt — turned the imagist fragment into a mythic epic of war, exile and female divinity, and her prose (HERmione, Tribute to Freud) is among the most experimental of the century. She is the poet through whom modernism becomes a woman's tradition.
stylistic_characteristics: The single crystalline image; the short free-verse line broken at the phrase; the Greek mask and the mythic persona; the hard, mineral vocabulary of sea, stone and flower; the absence of the article and the connective; the ecstatic repetition of the late long poems.
intellectual_concerns: The sea, the shore and the mineral world; Greek myth and the female god; war, the Blitz and the ruined city; exile, expatriation and the woman artist; the body, illness and analysis; the mother and the daughter; the sacred and the occult.
historical_significance: H. D. is the finest poet of Imagism and the founder of the modernist woman's epic: Sea Garden gave free verse its purest examples, Trilogy is one of the great poems of the Second World War, and Helen in Egypt rewrote the epic tradition from a woman's point of view. Her recovery in the 1970s and 1980s made her central to the modernist canon.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: British; the English rural lyric and the poetry of the threshold of war
literary_identity: Poet and essayist; the finest English nature poet of the century, who wrote almost all his poems in the last three years of his life and was killed at Arras.
biography: Born Philip Edward Thomas in Lambeth on 3 March 1878 to a Welsh father and an English mother; he read history at Oxford, married Helen Noble in 1899, and spent fifteen years as a prolific hack writer of reviews, country books and biographies — The Woodland Life (1897), The South Country (1909), Wales (1905) — in chronic depression and poverty. Encouraged by Robert Frost, whom he met in 1913, he began writing poems in December 1914; he enlisted in 1915, went to France in 1917, and was killed by a shell at Arras on 9 April 1917.
literary_profile: Thomas wrote the greatest English poems of the First World War that are not about the war: in three years he produced some 140 poems of the English countryside, of the road, the hedge, the bird and the passing of a way of life, in a quiet, unemphatic, perfectly weighted verse. His war poems — 'Rain', 'Lights Out', 'The Trumpet' — are among the finest in the language, and his prose is the foundation of the English nature essay of the century.
stylistic_characteristics: The plain, quiet, unrhymed or loosely rhymed line; the conversation held in the poem; the exact naming of plants, birds and places; the melancholy that never becomes rhetoric; the ending that simply stops; the prose of the country walk.
intellectual_concerns: England and the English countryside; the vanishing rural world and the coming of the road; solitude, depression and the burden of work; war, the soldier and the sense of doom; birds, weather and the seasons; the marriage and the unlived life.
historical_significance: Thomas is the finest English nature poet of the century and one of the great war poets: his 140 poems, written in three years, are among the permanent achievements of English verse, his prose founded the modern nature essay, and his death at Arras made him the period's symbol of the writer destroyed by the war he had enlisted to escape his own despair.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: British; the war poem of protest and the prose memoir of the trenches
literary_identity: Poet and memoirist; the war poet of anger and protest, and the author of the Sherston trilogy, the finest English prose memoir of the First World War.
biography: Born Siegfried Lorraine Sassoon at Matfield, Kent, on 8 September 1886 into a wealthy Anglo-Jewish family; he read history at Cambridge, hunted, played cricket and published privately financed verse before 1914. He served with the Royal Welch Fusiliers from 1915, was decorated, and in July 1917 threw his Military Cross into the Mersey and published 'A Soldier's Declaration' against the war; he was sent to Craiglockhart, where he met Wilfred Owen. He wrote the Sherston trilogy (1928–36), became a Catholic in 1957, and died at Heytesbury on 1 September 1967.
literary_profile: Sassoon is the great poet of protest of the First World War: his satirical war poems — 'They', 'Base Details', 'The General', 'Aftermath' — gave the anti-war movement its most quotable lines, and his meeting with Owen at Craiglockhart in 1917 changed the course of English war poetry. The Sherston trilogy is the finest prose memoir of the war and one of the great English autobiographies of the century.
stylistic_characteristics: The short satirical poem with a savage last line; colloquial speech and the officer's drawl; the sudden shift from anecdote to indictment; the rhyming couplet used as a weapon; the long prose memoir written with a novelist's eye for scene and a poet's ear for speech.
intellectual_concerns: War, protest, and the incompetence of the staff; the soldier and the rhetoric of sacrifice; courage, cowardice and the Military Cross; the English county families and the hunting field; memory and the reconstruction of a lost boyhood; pacifism and the conscience of the individual.
historical_significance: Sassoon is the central poet of protest of the First World War and one of its finest memoirists: his satirical poems made the anti-war case in the language of the mess and the trench, the Sherston trilogy is the great English war memoir, and his friendship with Owen made the greatest of the war poets possible.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: British; the trench lyric of pity and the pararhyme
literary_identity: Poet; the greatest of the First World War poets, killed a week before the armistice, whose poems became the central English statement about the pity of war.
biography: Born Wilfred Edward Salter Owen at Plas Wilmot, Oswestry, Shropshire, on 18 March 1893, the son of a railway clerk; he read at London University without taking a degree, taught English in Bordeaux (1913–15), and enlisted in the Artists' Rifles in 1915. He was commissioned in the Manchester Regiment, served on the Somme and at Serre, was blown up and spent 1917 in Craiglockhart, where Sassoon encouraged him; he returned to France in 1918, won the Military Cross, and was killed on the Sambre canal on 4 November 1918, a week before the armistice. His mother received the telegram as the bells were ringing.
literary_profile: Owen is the greatest poet of the First World War: in some two dozen finished poems he made the pity of war the subject of a lyric poetry that refuses both patriotism and despair. His technical invention — pararhyme, the half-comic half-horrified colloquialism, the long vowel held across an impossible rhyme — gave English poetry a new instrument, and 'Anthem for Doomed Youth', 'Dulce et Decorum Est' and 'Strange Meeting' are among the small number of poems every English reader knows by heart.
stylistic_characteristics: Pararhyme (graves/groves, killed/cold) as a structural device; the colloquial voice that can turn to prophecy; the exact and terrible physical detail; the sonnet and the irregular ode adapted to the trench; the pre-Raphaelite richness put to anti-heroic use; the ellipsis and the unfinished line.
intellectual_concerns: The pity of war and the waste of the young; the gas attack and the drowning man; the dead brother and the enemy met in hell; the church, the funeral and the mockery of the liturgy; the home front and the lie of the old rhetoric; comradeship and the doomed generation.
historical_significance: Owen is the greatest poet of the First World War and one of the most important English poets of the century: his two dozen finished poems changed the language of war poetry, his pararhyme gave modern verse a new technique, and 'Dulce et Decorum Est' and 'Strange Meeting' are permanent national texts. His preface — 'the Poetry is in the pity' — is the period's definitive statement about the poet's duty.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: Scottish; the novelist of the Scottish Renaissance and of the northern coast
literary_identity: Novelist; a leader of the Scottish Renaissance and the novelist of Caithness and the northern sea.
biography: Born Neil Miller Gunn at Dunbeath, Caithness, on 8 November 1891; he served in the customs service before The Grey Coast (1926) made him a novelist. Highland River (1937), Butcher's Broom (1939) and The Silver Darlings (1941) carried the Scottish Renaissance into the novel of the north, and his criticism of the movement made its case; he died at Dingwall on 15 January 1973.
literary_profile: Neil Gunn is the novelist of the Scottish Renaissance: The Grey Coast made the Caithness coast a world of the modern novel, Butcher's Broom carried the Clearances into the historical novel of the movement, and The Silver Darlings made the herring fishery the matter of the northern epic.
stylistic_characteristics: The prose of the northern coast and the sea, charged but plain; the clearance and the fishery as the memory of the north; the river and the inland water as the road of the self; the historical novel of the displaced people; the criticism of the Scottish renaissance.
intellectual_concerns: The north of Scotland and the Caithness coast; the Clearances and the displaced people; the herring fishery and the silver darlings; the Scottish Renaissance and the national novel; the river and the inland water of the self.

literary_identity: Novelist; the author of The Conquered, The Corn King and the Spring Queen and We Have Been Warned.
biography: Born Naomi Mary Margaret Haldane at Edinburgh on 1 November 1897, the sister of the biologist J. B. S. Haldane; she married the Labour lawyer Dick Mitchison and published The Conquered (1923), The Corn King and the Spring Queen (1931) and the socialist novel We Have Been Warned (1935). Her long career of the historical and the Scottish novel ran to the end of the century; she died at Tarbert, Argyll, on 11 January 1999.
literary_profile: Naomi Mitchison is the historical novelist of the Scottish renaissance and the socialist novelist of the thirties: The Corn King and the Spring Queen made the ancient world of Sparta and the corn king the matter of the modern historical novel, and We Have Been Warned carried the politics of the decade into the novel of the family.
stylistic_characteristics: The historical novel of the ancient world in the anthropologist's eye; the corn king and the ritual of the year; the socialist novel of the thirties in the family; the Scottish novel of Argyll; the plain prose of the argument and the rite.
intellectual_concerns: The ancient world and the ritual of the year; the conquered and the conqueror; socialism and the politics of the thirties; the family and the woman's work; Argyll and the Scottish west.
